B001257.text: This week, Representative Darren Soto and I introduced the “Federal Investment Restrictions on Equipment from Worrisome Authoritarian Linked Locations (FIREWALL) Act. This bipartisan legislation is designed to safeguard America's telecommunications infrastructure from foreign adversaries by prohibiting federal telecommunications funding from being used to purchase fiber-optic cable sourced from countries of concern. The legislation builds upon ongoing efforts to secure U.S. communications networks from foreign threats and prevent hostile regimes from gaining access to critical American infrastructure. America's telecommunications networks are the backbone of our economy, our national security, and our daily lives. As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in their efforts to infiltrate critical infrastructure, we must act proactively to protect our communications systems from potential vulnerabilities. The FIREWALL Actensures that taxpayer dollars are not used to subsidize technology sourced from countries that pose a threat to our national security. Rather than waiting until these products are deeply embedded in our networks and facing another costly 'rip and replace' effort, we should take commonsense steps now to prevent the problem from occurring in the first place.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. RT by @KenCalvert: “We the People.” Three enduring words that define America. As our nation marks 250 years, we honor the generations whose vision, sacrifice, and determination built the strongest, freest nation in history – and renew our responsibility to prepare it for those yet to come.

As America celebrates our 250th Anniversary this week, we’ve seen incredible patriotism on display in communities around the country. That same spirit was felt 50 years ago when we celebrated our bicentennial anniversary here in my hometown of Corona, and across the nation in 1976.  Corona High School student, Terri Smith, came up with the idea of painting a large mural on the Prado Dam spillway in Corona, and holding a high school contest to create a design for the mural. With the assistance of long-time Corona High activities director, Dave DiPaolo, Terri’s idea became a reality. At the end of the competition, a patriotic design drawn by students Ron Kammeyer and Perry Schaefer was selected. Terri then organized a group of roughly 30 student volunteers to paint the mural - which stretched 664 feet wide and 120 feet tall - using paint and supplies donated from local businesses. It was completed a few weeks before July 4, 1976. For decades, residents in the surrounding region took tremendous pride in the mural and its tribute to our great nation. As time passed, the mural suffered from neglect, weathering, and graffiti. Several unsuccessful attempts to restore the mural to its original glory were stymied. It was determined the original mural contained lead-based paint, which would require a complicated and expensive process to remove.  In 2022, after many twists and turns, the effort to restore the mural finally received a green light when the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which owns and operates the Prado Dam, granted the Bicentennial Freedom Mural Conservancy permission to repaint it. Thanks to the efforts of Riverside County Supervisor Karen Spiegel, the Conservancy in partnership with the Riverside County Flood Control District obtained the permits and other necessary requirements. The Conservancy also raised the money and obtained other donated resources to make the restoration possible.  Before the mural could be repainted, the lead-based paint from the old mural had to be removed by the Corps of Engineers. I was proud to secure $2.5 million in federal funding to make that removal possible. That removal process was completed by February 2023. The restored mural was painted and completed in the spring of 2023. On June 2, 2023, we held a celebration and ribbon cutting for the mural.  The Prado Dam Bicentennial Mural stands today as a vibrant reminder of our community’s love for our country. Like so many great American achievements, it was a collective effort, produced by many people coming together to achieve a common goal. The next time you drive past the mural, I hope you take a moment to give thanks to everyone who made it possible. God bless them, and may God continue to bless America.

For 39 years, Governor Bill Anoatubby has led my tribe, the Chickasaw Nation, with remarkable vision, a strategic hand, and unwavering dedication. His leadership has transformed not only the trajectory of the Nation, but the lives of the Chickasaw people.   Economically, his tenure has been nothing short of historic and unprecedented. Through Governor Anoatubby’s steady leadership, the Chickasaw Nation did more than just achieve its goals of economic development and self-sufficiency – it surpassed them. Under his guidance, the tribe evolved from dependence on federal funding to one that is self-sufficient and prosperous on its own. Today, thanks to him, the Chickasaw Nation supports more than 22,000 jobs and contributes $3.7 billion annually to Oklahoma’s economy, including $1.2 billion in wages and benefits.   However, Governor Anoatubby’s impact cannot be measured by just economics. Throughout his lengthy tenure, he also placed a significant emphasis on preserving and sharing the precious heritage of the Chickasaw Nation. Through initiatives such as the Chickasaw Nation Division of Arts and Humanities and the Chickasaw Cultural Center, he ensured that our history, language, arts, and culture would continue to inspire future generations.   These achievements, on top of many others, make it unmistakably clear: Governor Bill Anoatubby is the most consequential Chickasaw Nation leader since the removal period. And his influence has extended past just the Chickasaw Nation. His leadership and impact are respected by every Oklahoman.   For nearly four decades, Governor Anoatubby has embodied true commitment to the Chickasaw people and Oklahoma. The powerful combination of his leadership, vision, and generosity has allowed all of us in our state to shape a brighter future for ourselves and all those touched by the results of his leadership. On a personal level, I am fortunate to call Governor Anoatubby a mentor and a trusted friend.   His retirement is an enormous loss for the Chickasaw Nation, all Indian Country, and the state of Oklahoma. However, he leaves the tribe stronger than he found it, as he hands it off to his very competent and bright son, Chris, the Lieutenant Governor. I have no doubt Chris will carry on his father’s legacy with wisdom, competence, and care, and I look forward to seeing everything the future holds for the Chickasaw Nation.   In conclusion, to Governor Anoatubby, congratulations on a truly remarkable career and a lifetime of service. Thank you for your leadership, your vision, your friendship, and the legacy you leave behind. I wish you, Janice, and your entire family the best as you enter this next chapter.

C001063.text: This week in Washington, I introduced a resolution recognizing Laredo's 271st anniversary, voted to pass the KIDS Act, and announced $25 million in federal funding for the World Trade Bridge Expansion Project. The World Trade Bridge grant is a major investment in Laredo and South Texas. It will help expand one of the country's busiest commercial crossings, reduce congestion, and support the trade and jobs that depend on this critical port of entry. I'll continue working to bring federal resources back to South Texas and support the priorities of communities across TX-28.

Housing costs remain one of the biggest challenges facing families in South Texas. As http://Realtor.com reported, new-home sales have slowed, builders are being cautious with new construction, and mortgage rates remain high. When fewer homes are being built and borrowing costs stay high, it becomes harder for families to find a home they can afford. That is why I voted to pass the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. This bill takes practical steps to cut unnecessary delays, support new housing construction, improve federal housing programs, and help expand affordable housing. No single bill will fix the housing market overnight, but increasing housing supply is an important part of lowering costs. I will continue working with both parties to make housing more affordable for families in #TX28. https://www.mysanantonio.com/realestate/article/congress-aims-to-lower-housing-costs-with-new-22322752.php

A construction site should not be sitting empty because workers are afraid to show up. Families in South Texas need housing, businesses need workers, and our communities need projects like this to move forward. I have long supported strong border security, but enforcement should be targeted at criminals and real threats to public safety. When workers are scared, projects get delayed, costs go up, and local economies feel it. We need smart, targeted enforcement that keeps our communities safe without hurting the workers, families, and businesses that help build South Texas.

Big news for Laredo and South Texas: I secured a $25,000,000 federal BUILD grant for the World Trade Bridge Expansion Project. This is a major investment for the most important trade crossing in the country. The World Trade Bridge supports jobs, commerce, and supply chains across South Texas and the nation, and this funding will help make sure our infrastructure keeps up with growing trade. The project will add two lanes to the existing bridge and construct a new, separate span with eight northbound lanes, helping reduce congestion and strengthen the movement of goods through Laredo and Webb County. A formal announcement with Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño and the Laredo City Council will follow. I’ll continue delivering federal dollars to #TX28 and support the infrastructure projects that keep South Texas moving.

K000375.text: On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

M001153.text: The Supreme Court’s decision today recognizes that states face unique circumstances in administering their elections. In Alaska, voting is not as simple as driving down the road to a neighborhood polling place. Many Alaskans live in remote communities that are not connected to the road system, requiring ballots to travel by bush plane or boat, which means volatile weather conditions and limited infrastructure can determine whether those ballots arrive on time. Even with Alaska’s current 10-day grace period for in-state ballots, we have seen mail delays cause legally cast ballots to arrive too late to be counted. Today’s decision affirms that states have the flexibility to account for these realities and helps ensure that every American who lawfully casts a ballot has the opportunity to have it counted. https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-mailed-ballots-trump-elections-5f24f718ea92a33838485ce6302e079e

W000808.text: Museums exist to preserve the truth, not serve the politics of any administration. You cannot make America greater by erasing the people who helped build it. Black history is American history and must remain free from political interference. Hands off our Smithsonian.

Today, we honor the anniversary of the Civil Rights Act, a defining moment in our nation’s history that brought us closer to the promise of equal justice under the law. This victory was earned through courage and sacrifice, and its legacy lives on through our commitment to justice, equality, and opportunity for all.

Our history is not up for political negotiation. The Smithsonian must remain independent from political interference by the Executive Branch. For nearly a century, Americans fought to establish the National Museum of African American History and Culture because we understood that Black history is American history. We cannot allow anyone to rewrite the truth or erase the generations whose sacrifices built this institution.

As America approaches its 250th anniversary, we should be expanding opportunities to learn from our history, not restricting them. The Smithsonian belongs to the American people, and the National Museum of African American History and Culture belongs to every child who deserves to see themselves reflected in our nation's story.

Team Peters has lost a talented and tenacious member of our alumni family after a years-long battle with cancer. Kelly Davis was an award-winning journalist who served as our Press Secretary from 2023-2024. For several years before she joined the office, we admired Kelly’s skill in writing stories that made a difference for our region – about homelessness, housing affordability, and criminal justice reform. Investigative reporting was her calling, and her work led to new state laws that have made California a more just and transparent place for everyone. It was an honor that she came to work with us. We appreciated the history, depth, and context she brought to the role of Press Secretary, as well as the kind, compassionate demeanor she brought to the team. We learned from her quiet maturity. She taught us more about how journalism and storytelling work and we taught her a little about how government ought to function; we gained invaluable insights from each other. Today, we’re especially remembering our staff retreat in Washington, D.C. that year. She was a lot of fun on that trip! When she felt called back to journalism, we understood and knew that she would continue to shine a light on injustice and give a voice to those who needed it. She did just that for as long as she could. Our community has lost a trusted source of information and a fierce advocate for change. We will miss her deeply and send Kelly’s loved ones our warmest condolences.

W000821.text: Arkansas, and the United States, have an incredibly abundant source of timber. Unfortunately, we look to nations outside of our borders to supply us with a resource that we have right here in our own back yard. Healthy forest management is more than just taking care of our trees, in fact we have been loving our trees to death. Our forests are overstocked and unhealthy because we have no markets for the wood and rural communities are suffering because their resource and economic opportunity are tied directly to the forests. A nation with such an abundance of timber should never be reliant on other countries to import lumber and pulp products, but that’s where we find ourselves.  Recently, we’ve seen paper mills across the country closing – even a few here in the Fourth District. With a background in Forestry and Engineering, Congressman Westerman understands just how important our pulp and paper industry is and he remains heavily focused on legislation that will support such an important economic contributer for Arkansas. This week’s meeting with the Pulp & Paperworkers’ Resource Council to discuss just how important the forest products industry underscored the need for Congress to work diligently to provide its support.

F000466.text: Yesterday, inside Independence Hall, I was grateful to share such a profoundly American and historic moment with my friend and neighbor, @RepHoulahan, alongside a bipartisan group of our colleagues. Standing in the very place where, 250 years ago, patriots chose independence and set our nation on the course of liberty, we were reminded that America’s promise has never been carried forward by one generation, one party, or one person alone. It has always depended on citizens willing to come together in service of something larger than themselves—a nation born not from sameness, but from conviction; not from ease, but from courage; not from division, but from the enduring belief that free people could build something worthy together. As we mark America 250, may we honor that spirit and carry forward, together, the sacred work of this truly great nation.

Happy 92nd Birthday to my amazing Dad, Jim Fitzpatrick!! A Korean War veteran. A devoted husband, father of eight, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The quiet strength of our family, and one of the greatest blessings of my life. To know him is to know a good man in the truest and most enduring American sense of the word: faithful in duty, generous in spirit, humble in service, and constant in love. I am blessed and proud beyond measure to call him my Dad. Please join me in wishing him a very happy 92nd birthday!

On the eve of America’s 250th Birthday, I can think of no better way to honor our nation’s birthday than by celebrating one of the Americans—one of our true Hometown Heroes—who helped preserve the freedom we celebrate and embody the greatness we inherit.. Meet Robert Stephenson of Southampton, a World War II Veteran, whom I had the honor of spending time with on his 101st birthday. He is still active. Still sharp. Still strong. Still proud. Still carrying himself with the quiet dignity of a generation that embodied service, sacrifice, and patriotism. Born on June 14, 1925—Flag Day— Robert entered the world under the very symbol he would one day serve. He came of age during the Great Depression, in an America that knew hardship, sacrifice, uncertainty, and resolve. It was a time that tested families, formed character, and forged a generation that would be called upon to save the world. At just 17 years old, Robert answered that call and enlisted in the United States Navy in 1943. He served honorably during World War II as a Yeoman with Photographic Squadron VD-2 in the Pacific Theater, managing the personnel and aerial mapping records that supported critical operations in one of the most consequential fights for freedom in human history. And when the war was won, Robert came home and continued to build the country he had helped preserve. He studied accounting at night through the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. He founded RL Stephenson Incorporated in 1964. He built a respected business, created opportunity, raised a family, and lived by the timeless American virtues of honesty, fairness, perseverance, humility, and respect for others. With his beloved wife, Helene, he shared 75 years of marriage and built a legacy that now lives on through children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. Tomorrow, we celebrate 250 years since our great nation declared to the world the revolutionary truth at the heart of America: that all are created equal, liberty comes from God and not government, and free people can govern themselves. That promise endures because generations of Americans have defended it, strengthened it, and made it real. Americans like Robert Stephenson. May we always honor America’s greatness and remember that it lives only in monuments or history books. It lives in people like Robert—in their courage, their decency, their sacrifice, their faithfulness, and their lifelong love and service to community and country. Please join me in wishing Southampton’s own Robert Stephenson a very happy 101st birthday, thanking him for his extraordinary service, and honoring all the Americans whose example still calls us, 250 years later, to be worthy of the nation they helped preserve.

250 years ago, in Philadelphia, our Founders gathered to declare a truth that would change the course of history: that our rights come not from government, but from God; that all are created equal; and that liberty is both America’s inheritance and America’s calling. Today, I had the profound honor of standing in their footsteps at Independence Hall, alongside a bipartisan delegation of my colleagues and Governor Shapiro, to deliver the opening invocation as our nation prepares to mark America’s 250th year. To stand in that hallowed hall— where an idea became a Declaration, where conviction became a Republic, and where the work of America began—was a moment I will never forget. At this historic threshold, may we look back with gratitude and forward with renewed commitment to the sacred charge entrusted to every generation: to remain one people, bound by one Republic, and called to carry America’s promise forward together. My sincere thanks to my friends and partners, @CongBoyle and @RepJeffries, for the hosting this historic occasion.

Today in Historic Bristol Borough, we honored one of the quiet beginnings of the American story. In 1775, before our independence was won and before our Constitution was written, the Second Continental Congress established a national postal system under Benjamin Franklin, our first Postmaster General. Bristol was chosen as one of the original 61 Postal Service offices—a vital link on the route between Philadelphia and New York at a time when communication was not a convenience, but a lifeline for liberty. Through revolution and reunion, war and peace, hardship and prosperity, the Bristol Borough Post Office has carried more than mail. It has carried news from home, word from the front, notices of birth and loss, commerce for small businesses, and the daily threads that bind neighbors, families, and a nation together. That is the beauty of this anniversary. It reminds us that America was built not only by the names etched in marble, but by generations of citizens and public servants who did their duty faithfully, quietly, and well. For 250 years, the men and women of the Bristol Borough Post Office have served this community with dedication and pride. And across our nation, postal workers continue that same essential mission every day, connecting Americans from the largest cities to the smallest towns, from one doorstep to the next. As we continue marching towards America’s 250th birthday, please join me in thanking every incredible postal worker who has served Historic Bristol Borough across these two and a half centuries, and all of America’s postal workers who continue to keep our communities, our commerce, and our country connected. Their service is honorable, and their legacy is deeply American.

Friday in the First Meet Wrenn Phillips, the Town Crier of Halifax and one of the community's most dedicated stewards of American history. For decades, Wrenn has faithfully carried forward a centuries-old tradition, lending his voice, his passion, and his unwavering commitment to the annual Halifax Resolves commemoration and countless historic events that celebrate our nation's founding. Dressed in authentic 18th-century attire, Wrenn proudly rings his bell and proclaims, "Hear ye! Hear ye!"—inviting all who gather to step back in time and remember the extraordinary courage of those who dared to pursue liberty. With every proclamation, he transforms history into a living experience, reminding visitors why Halifax is recognized as the Birthplace of American Independence. On April 12, 1776, the Halifax Resolves marked the first official action by an American colony authorizing its delegates to the Continental Congress to concur with the other colonies in declaring independence from Great Britain. Through his dedication to preserving this remarkable legacy, Wrenn inspires new generations to honor the sacrifices, vision, and determination that secured our independence. Wrenn's service is far more than a ceremonial role; it is a calling. Year after year, he has devoted himself to ensuring that one of the defining stories of our nation's founding continues to educate, inspire, and unite all who hear it. His steadfast commitment reflects the enduring ideals of patriotism, perseverance, civic pride, and love of country that have shaped our nation from its earliest days. As America commemorates 250 years of independence, Wrenn Phillips reminds us that history endures because of faithful individuals who dedicate themselves to preserving and sharing it with future generations. We are profoundly grateful for his decades of exemplary service, his unwavering devotion to Halifax's extraordinary story, and his tireless efforts to ensure that North Carolina's proud legacy as "First in Freedom" continues to echo across our state and throughout our nation. #FridaySpotlight
As we join in celebrating the spirit of America, we are stronger together. 🇺🇸

“In God We Trust” is a phrase woven throughout American life. It is recited in the Pledge of Allegiance, printed on our currency, etched in the House Chamber, and recognized as our nation’s official motto. This principle has long influenced American history. Our Creator is referenced in the Declaration of Independence as the source of our unalienable rights and inherent dignity. Many of the Founding Fathers were shaped by Christian beliefs and biblical principles, which heavily influenced their understanding of human nature, morality, liberty, and self-government. George Washington is said to have prayed for divine guidance during the Revolutionary War, and President John Adams famously wrote, “Our Constitution was made only for a moral and religious people. It is wholly inadequate to the government of any other.” As we celebrate 250 years of our nation’s history, we are reminded that our greatest strength does not come from government or human achievement alone. The blessings we enjoy and the freedoms we cherish are gifts that require humility, gratitude, and faith. Just as generations before us sought God’s guidance, we must continue to rely on Him as we face the challenges and opportunities of the future. IN GOD WE TRUST! “Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom He has chosen for His own inheritance.” — Psalm 33:12

I recently had the opportunity to visit the XPRIZE Wildfire competition at Nenana Airport alongside Cathy Cahill, Director of the Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration. It was impressive to see firsthand how innovators are developing autonomous technologies that can detect and respond to wildfires faster than ever before. As Alaska faces increasingly challenging wildfire seasons, early detection and rapid response can mean the difference between a small ignition and a devastating fire that threatens critical infrastructure, and natural resources. The recent wildfire activity near Anderson and Clear Space Force Station highlights exactly why these innovations matter. Investing in cutting-edge technology, strengthening our wildfire preparedness, and improving forest management must remain national priorities. That is why I am proud to co-sponsor the Fix Our Forests Act and support the work of the House Natural Resources Committee, which has made wildfire prevention and forest resilience a key priority this Congress. By combining responsible forest management with emerging technologies, we can reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfires and better support our first responders. Thank you to the teams competing in Alaska, Cathy Cahill and her team, and everyone working to advance solutions that will help keep Alaskans safe.

On this day in 1944, over 34,000 American soldiers crowded together in small, amphibious boats en route to Omaha Beach. As the boats landed on the beach, and their bow ramps dropped down leading the men ashore, unrelenting machine gun fire rained down from enemy bunkers. Undeterred, the American and Allied forces emerged from the battle victorious, but not without a heavy cost. Over 2,500 Americans died at Omaha Beach. One of them was 1st Lieutenant Thomas Royce Dallas Jr. from our Congressional District in Griffin, Georgia, who drew his last breath on the shores of Omaha Beach. As we remember the heroism Americans exhibited on D-Day and we reflect on the cost of freedom, may we remember and be inspired by the names and faces of those brave soldiers who died in service to our Country.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: La France a déployé au Moyen-Orient des moyens de déminage, avec notamment deux chasseurs de mines. Accompagnés de deux frégates et d’un avion de patrouille maritime, ces moyens sont prêts à contribuer, avec nos partenaires, à la pleine reprise de la navigation et à garantir la sécurité du trafic dans le détroit d’Ormuz. La signature, le 17 juin dernier, du mémorandum d’accord entre les États-Unis et l’Iran constitue une avancée importante en faveur de la stabilité régionale, en réaffirmant notamment la liberté de navigation dans le détroit d’Ormuz. Compte tenu de cette évolution favorable et de l’évolution des besoins, à l’issue des échanges constructifs que j’ai eus avec le Sultan d’Oman, j’ai décidé d’adapter notre dispositif. Le porte-avions Charles de Gaulle rejoint ainsi son port d’attache à Toulon, tandis que nos moyens de déminage et leur escorte demeurent déployés et prêts à intervenir avec nos partenaires. La France reste pleinement mobilisée et continuera d’ajuster ses moyens en fonction de l’évolution de la situation et des besoins de sécurité dans la région.
